rationale: A wins because it separates the real beats instead of squeezing the bank claim until it squeaks: "Who holds the keys: what customer-managed encryption actually protects against" is a security story that can stand even if the bank names do not. B has competent shapes, but "Four of the five largest US banks are quietly testing Notion" leans on a fragile, unnamed customer claim and adds drama the update did not supply. A also catches the offline engineering angle B throws away as "a bare feature description."
gaps_in_A: "A cloud-native workspace is rebuilding for the offline case it spent a decade dismissing" imports a decade-long Notion attitude the update never gave you.
"Notion against Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace" is plausible competitive context, but the update gives no bake-off, replacement, or competitor proof.
"compliance features are usually a paid tier — sovereignty as an upsell is standard practice" needs evidence before it becomes a money angle; otherwise it is a newsletter take in a reporter costume.
gaps_in_B: "quietly testing" is invented color. The update says the banks run pilots, not that the pilots are quiet, secret, or deliberately under the radar.
"historically seen as too lightweight" and "consumer-rooted software" import market baggage not present in the update.

"Notion lets EU and Australian enterprise customers keep their data at home" overstates data residency before proving what is covered: backups, logs, telemetry, support access, and derived data all matter.

Refusing "Notion ships offline-first editing" as "a bare feature description" misses the real engineering/local-first angle: offline edit plus sync-on-reconnect at roughly 100M-user scale is not just a feature blurb.
